title: Bond returns vs. stock returns
subtitle: Bonds vs stocks return comparison
openingQuestion: Over the long run (20-30 years), why do stocks usually deliver a higher average return than bonds?
openingOptions: Because stocks always rise at a fixed, predetermined rate every year, with no real-world exception in the stock market
Because shareholders bear higher risk, so they're compensated with an equity risk premium
Because stocks are inherently far lower risk than bonds at every stage of the financial market, even when a company goes bankrupt
Because current law reserves bonds solely for large institutional investors, and individuals are entirely barred from trading them
explanation: A basic finance principle: higher risk must come with a higher expected return, or no one would accept that risk. Because shareholders bear more risk than bondholders (no fixed interest, and a total loss if the company goes bankrupt), the market compensates with a higher average expected return over the long run - even though stocks can still post heavy losses in any given year.

realWorldExample.company: The VN-Index compared with the 10-year government bond rate
realWorldExample.description: Looking back over the past 20 years, the VN-Index (representing Vietnam's stock market) has delivered an estimated average annual return of about 10-12%/year (including dividends), despite deep drops such as 2008 (down over 60%) or 2022 (down over 30%). Meanwhile, the 10-year government bond delivered a stable yield of only around 3-5%/year over the same period, but has almost never posted a loss when held to maturity. This clearly illustrates the trade-off between a higher return (with larger swings) and a lower return (with stability).

quiz.question: What is the 'equity risk premium'?
options: The personal income tax due when receiving a dividend
The brokerage fee paid to a securities firm when buying
The higher expected return that compensates for equity risk, so the coupon payment functions no differently than a company's discretionary dividend
Extra money a company pays to long-tenured shareholders
quiz.explanation: The equity risk premium is the gap between a stock's expected return and the risk-free yield (usually benchmarked against a government bond). It's the reward investors demand for accepting the higher risk of investing in stocks.

quiz.question: An investor says: 'I'll only invest in stocks because they always earn more than bonds every year.' Is this correct?
options: Correct, because bonds earn nothing for the holder
Incorrect, because new bonds always earn more than stocks
Correct, stocks beat bonds in every single year
Incorrect - stocks only beat bonds on average over the long run, and this only holds true when both firms belong to the exact same industry sector
quiz.explanation: The stock advantage only shows up clearly when looking at average returns over a long span (10-20-30 years). In the short run, stocks can swing sharply and post far heavier losses than bonds in any given year.

quiz.question: During periods like 2008 or 2022, how did an all-stock portfolio differ from a 60/40 portfolio?
options: The 60/40 portfolio fell less, because the bond portion cushioned the drop
Both fell by the exact same amount, since a crisis drags every asset down equally
The 60/40 portfolio fell harder, because bonds always lose value faster than stocks, which is exactly opposite to what happened when the two asset classes were compared in 2008
The all-stock portfolio rose, because investors poured money into cheap stocks
quiz.explanation: That's why people accept a lower expected yield to hold bonds. Note that 2022 was a memorable exception: rapidly rising rates pushed both stocks and bonds down together, and that cushion was thinner than usual.

quiz.question: In developed markets, how large is the equity risk premium usually, per year?
options: About 20-25%, meaning stocks earn many times what government bonds do
About 4-6% above the government bond yield, averaged over the long run
About 0.5%, too small to be worth accepting extra risk for, a point that trips up many beginners
It can't be measured, since this figure changes completely randomly each year
quiz.explanation: Long-run studies usually find a level of 4-6%/year. That number sounds modest, but compounded over 30 years it creates a difference of several times in the final balance - which is why someone with plenty of time is advised to prioritize stocks.

quiz.question: Why is the stock advantage only reliable over the long run, not year by year?
options: Because a stock is only allowed to pay a dividend after being held for a full ten consecutive years
Because the risk premium is only paid out by regulators at the end of each ten-year cycle
Because short-term volatility is huge, and in many years stocks lose more than bonds
Because in the short run, stocks consistently and reliably earn less than bonds, something worth double-checking in practice
quiz.explanation: The risk premium is an average, not a yearly guarantee. There are years when stocks fall 30% while bonds stay positive. That very uncertainty is why the premium exists - if winning were guaranteed, no one would call it risk.

quiz.question: A 60-year-old asks: 'So should I just put everything into stocks to capture the risk premium?'
options: Yes, because the risk premium applies equally to every investor at every age
No, because people over 60 are legally barred from holding stocks
Yes, as long as the stocks chosen pay a high, steady dividend
No - the premium only becomes real if there's enough time to wait out downturns
quiz.explanation: The equity risk premium is the reward for enduring volatility, and enduring it takes time. Someone about to withdraw money doesn't have that time - for them, a deep drop isn't a chapter in the middle of the story, it's the ending.

keyTakeaways: Stocks usually earn a higher average return than bonds over the long run, to compensate for higher risk - called the equity risk premium
The stock return advantage is only clear over the long run; in the short run, stocks can absolutely lose more than bonds
Bonds deliver a lower yield but one that's far more stable and predictable - which is why both have a distinct role in a portfolio

practicePrompt.question: In 2022, the VN-Index fell over 30% while government bonds kept paying interest steadily. Looking only at 2022 in isolation, which conclusion about comparing stocks and bonds is correct?
options: In 2022 bonds outperformed stocks, but that doesn't disprove stocks being higher over the long run
Stocks are always better than bonds every year, including 2022, since this is just a passing event not worth noting
The 2022 result proves bonds are always the better choice over any long-term investment horizon going forward
No conclusion can be drawn from any single year at all, since one year's data is entirely meaningless
practicePrompt.explanation: The equity risk premium is only clear when viewed over the long run - a specific year like 2022 can absolutely go the opposite way without disproving the long-term trend.

application.title: Compare expected yields
application.message: Write down the long-run average return you expect from stocks and from a bond you're considering, then ask yourself whether that gap is enough to compensate for the stock's higher risk.
application.secondary: Putting the two numbers side by side makes the allocation decision clearer.

sections.text: If bonds are safer and more stable, why doesn't everyone just invest in bonds? The answer lies in the most fundamental trade-off in finance: higher risk must come with a higher expected return.
Why stocks 'have to' earn more over the long run

Shareholders stand behind bondholders in the order of payment - if a company goes bankrupt, bondholders get paid first, and shareholders only get what's left (often very little or nothing). Shareholders also don't get a fixed return like a bond coupon - their return depends entirely on whether the business does well or poorly. Because this risk is much larger than being a creditor, investors won't put money into stocks unless they expect a significantly higher average return than bonds - otherwise everyone would simply choose the safer bond.

sections.text: A higher average return doesn't mean winning every year

This is where many newcomers get it wrong. 'Stocks earn more than bonds' is true when looking at a 15-20-30 year average, but is completely wrong applied to any specific year. In 2022, the VN-Index fell more than 30%, while government bonds kept paying interest exactly as promised. Anyone fully invested in stocks that year and forced to withdraw right at the bottom took a heavy hit, while bondholders were unaffected.

sections.label: A practical lesson
sections.text: A stock's higher return only 'pays out' to those patient enough to hold through volatile periods without panic-selling. If you're not sure you can handle watching your account drop 30% in a year, you may need a higher bond allocation to sleep well.

So the question isn't 'should I choose stocks or bonds', but rather understanding the trade-off between the two asset types well enough to allocate a proportion that fits your own goals, investment horizon, and risk tolerance.

lines: Stocks earn more than bonds over the long run because investors demand a reward for the higher risk.
But that advantage only shows up over many years, not every year - and only for those patient enough not to sell during a downturn.
